title: Emergency Braking and Recovery Principles
summary: Recognize when emergency braking is used and what a driver should monitor after it is commanded.
objectives: Explain why recovery follows equipment-specific rules

sections.heading: Purpose of emergency braking
sections.body: Emergency braking is a safety function for abnormal or hazardous situations requiring an urgent stop. It is separate from routine service-brake regulation. The response can include traction cut-off and a high-priority brake application, depending on the vehicle.

sections.heading: Commands and indications
sections.body: The master-controller EB detent and separate Security Brake pushbutton initiate emergency braking. The Emergency Brake Release control is distinct from these activation controls. Monitor the EB indication and the speedometer to confirm deceleration.

sections.heading: Observe the response
sections.body: After an emergency request, monitor whether speed decreases and whether the emergency indication remains active. An emergency command must not be treated as proof of immediate zero speed.

sections.heading: Recovery is not automatic
sections.body: After standstill, the TRAINEX simulation requires master handle N and a deliberate Emergency Brake Release command; its release period is modeled as three seconds. Actual recovery follows the train operator’s rules and is not necessarily equivalent.

reviewQuestions.question: Is emergency braking intended for normal speed regulation?
choices: No, service braking is used for normal deceleration
reviewQuestions.explanation: Service braking is used for controlled routine slowing; emergency braking is for abnormal situations.

reviewQuestions.question: What confirms that an emergency request has brought the train to a standstill?
reviewQuestions.explanation: An emergency request does not cause instantaneous standstill; the driver must observe the resulting response.
